describe.name: Block fixture (test)
principles: Work tolerance is most trainable characteristic
Fit for whatever comes next not peaked in one domain
Maintain 60 to 70 pct across all fitness domains
Hard day followed by recovery day
Power endurance and strength endurance over max strength
Reduce rest periods or increase weight not both simultaneously

blocks.headline: 5 min
blocks.note: 5-min targeted prep: thoracic rotation, ankle dorsiflexion, and hip hinge with dowel. Power clean requires full thoracic extension and rack position (front squat depth). Check wrist mobility for rack position.
blocks.title: Movement prep

blocks.note: 5 × 3 power clean or hang power clean at 70-80% of power clean max. Bar speed is the priority metric — if bar speed slows, stop the set. Selector upgrades novice athletes (hang power clean) to power clean as they accumulate sessions. Reset to the floor each rep; do not touch-and-go — this is a power session, not conditioning.
blocks.title: Primary power pull

blocks.note: Push press 4 × 5 at working weight. Push press (leg drive) is preferred over strict press for a power session — the leg drive trains rate of force development through the kinetic chain. Load: the bar should move explosively. If you cannot use leg drive to initiate bar movement, reduce load.
blocks.title: Overhead press power

blocks.note: Romanian deadlift or conventional deadlift 3 × 8 at moderate load. Posterior chain reinforcement — not the primary focus of this session, so load is sub-maximal. Controlled eccentric (3 sec down).
blocks.title: Posterior chain accessory

u99beef23_barbell_power_complex.name: Barbell Power Complex (Olympic Lift Derivatives)
u99beef23_barbell_power_complex.note: Barbell power development session built around Olympic lift derivatives: power clean, hang power clean, push press, and pull. These movements develop rate of force development and neuromuscular power in a way that carries over to athletic performance and GPP. Gym Jones uses power cleans as an integral part of strength training — not for competition but for the athletic quality they develop. Load is submaximal; bar speed is the quality metric. Technique prerequisite: athletes must be competent at the hip hinge pattern before performing power cleans. At novice level, default to KB ballistic session instead. Intermediate+ athletes are cleared for barbell power work. Rest fully between power sets (3-4 min) — power drops immediately when fatigue accumulates. Do not rush warm-up sets.

blocks.headline: Every minute × 10
blocks.note: One rep per minute for 10 minutes. Default movement is back squat or deadlift. Load wave: start at 85%, build to 92–95% by set 5, descend to 85–87% by set 10. If any rep looks or feels poor, reduce load and hold there; no grinding.
blocks.title: Primary emom lift

u99beef23_emom_strength.name: EMOM Strength Wave (10×1)
u99beef23_emom_strength.note: Ten singles on the minute at 85–95% 1RM. Each interval is one rep; the remainder of the 60-second window is rest. This format accumulates near-maximal neural stimulus (10 singles = high CNS exposure) while total volume is low and fatigue is managed via the enforced rest window. Effective for peaking and for pushing a 1RM up without high injury risk from max-effort singles. Load can wave across intervals: e.g., 85/87/90/92/95/92/90/90/87/85%. Bar is loaded and staged before the clock starts. Typically follows a brief barbell warm-up; do not precede with heavy volume work.

u99beef23_gym_jones_accumulation.name: Gym Jones Accumulation Circuit (Goblet Squat / Bear Crawl / Carry)
u99beef23_gym_jones_accumulation.note: Gym Jones accumulation-style circuit combining a high-rep squat movement, locomotion, and a loaded carry. Emphasis on total volume and time under load rather than maximal intensity. Used as a GPP conditioning day between heavier strength sessions. Movements cycle through lower push, locomotion, and carry patterns. Rest is minimal between movements; take 2–3 min between rounds. Target: 3–5 rounds depending on fitness level.

blocks.note: 60 min continuous, Zone 1-2. Conversational throughout: if you cannot hold a sentence, you are working too hard and this has stopped being a recovery session. Duration scales to the athlete's budget; intensity never does.

u99beef23_gym_jones_aerobic_recovery.name: Gym Jones Aerobic Recovery (Row / Swim / Ruck)
u99beef23_gym_jones_aerobic_recovery.note: Gym Jones recovery-day format: 60-120 min of easy, continuous, low-impact work at conversational pace. The purpose is circulation and aerobic development between hard sessions, not additional stress — Twight's rule is that the recovery day must actually recover, and an athlete who turns it into a third hard session loses the following week. Row is the default (Concept II is the house ergometer); swim and ruck are equally valid. Damper 4-6, 18-22 SPM.

u99beef23_gym_jones_breathing_ladder.name: Gym Jones KB Breathing Ladder (1–20–1)
u99beef23_gym_jones_breathing_ladder.note: Gym Jones breathing ladder: perform 1 KB swing, take 1 breath, perform 2 swings, take 2 breaths... climb to 20, descend back to 1. Total: ~400 swings. The breath count equals the rep count — this enforces structured, complete recovery between micro-sets. Not a conditioning WOD; it is a test of mental endurance and breath management under cumulative fatigue. KB weight: 24 kg (53 lb) for trained athletes; scale down to 16 kg for early intermediate. Mark Twight: "The breathing ladder is a test of will as much as fitness." Warm up with the same bell at 1–5–1 before the full ladder.

u99beef23_gym_jones_circuit.name: Gym Jones Operator Circuit
u99beef23_gym_jones_circuit.note: Gym Jones Strength Day format as described in Operator Fitness I/II. Structure: warm-up complex → primary strength work → core/skill block → conditioning finisher. This is not a conditioning-only session — it is the Gym Jones definition of a "strength day," which always includes a structural finisher to build work tolerance alongside neural strength. The barbell complex warm-up (Six-Way or DB equivalent) primes the movement patterns and elevates heart rate before the primary strength lift. Core block includes TGU and plank/FLR. Finisher is a timed rowing piece for systemic endurance. Mark Twight: "We value horsepower ahead of appearance." This format delivers both. Rest: 3–5 min between heavy barbell sets, 1–2 min between complex sets.

u99beef23_gym_jones_row_intervals.name: Gym Jones Row Intervals (6 × 500 m)
u99beef23_gym_jones_row_intervals.note: Gym Jones rowing interval session: 6 × 500 m on the ergometer with 3-min active rest between efforts. One of the most reliable power-endurance tests and builders in the Gym Jones canon. Stimulus is anaerobic threshold to VO2max — athletes should sustain a pace close to their 2000m race-pace split. Target splits narrow over the program cycle; consistency across intervals is the primary goal (don't go out too hot on interval 1). Mark Twight: "Row hard. You can't fake the erg." The rower provides objective, unfalsifiable data — use it to track progress.

blocks.note: 10×5 TGU alternating sides (or 10×10 if counting per arm). Use a light bell — this is recovery, not strength. Rest 60–90 sec between sets. Focus on positional quality at each pause point: floor press, half-kneeling, standing. Reach 100 total reps.
blocks.title: Tgu volume

u99beef23_gym_jones_tgu_recovery.name: Gym Jones TGU Recovery (100 Total Reps)
u99beef23_gym_jones_tgu_recovery.note: Gym Jones recovery session: 100 total Turkish Get-Up reps at a sub-maximal load (typically 16 kg for advanced athletes; 12 kg for intermediate). Performed at a slow, deliberate pace — this is restorative, not conditioning. Each rep demands full shoulder stability, hip flexor mobility, and joint integrity through a complex multi-position movement. The high rep count at low load flushes the tissues without adding stress load. Twight on TGU recovery: "Movement quality under fatigue. The fatigue reveals the compensation patterns." Take all the rest you need — the goal is 100 quality reps, not speed.

describe.summary: Six-day week: 3 key sessions (strength, circuit, accumulation), 2 recovery sessions, 1 long endurance, 1 full rest. Intensity model is hard/easy alternation — not polarized (no 80/20 split), but structured hard-day/recovery-day cycling. Progression levers are deliberate: reduce rest (bodyweight work) OR increase load (barbell/KB), never both simultaneously. Excessive max strength / max speed development is explicitly de-emphasized; power-endurance and strength-endurance are the primary targets. Operator context: relative strength + aerobic capacity + mental durability. Programs are 1-month blocks, repeatable 2–3× or cycled between Operator I / Operator II.

tracks.description: Twight's sequential blocks for operator fitness: accumulate volume, convert it to intensity, then realise it. Each block is about a month; the cycle repeats.
tracks.name: Block Periodization Program

phases.deload: Every 4 weeks an easier week, keeping 60 % of the volume.
phases.description: A month of high volume at moderate intensity on the six-day week: strength, circuit and accumulation key days, recovery days between them, one long endurance day. Power-endurance and strength-endurance are the targets; maximal strength and speed are not chased.
phases.name: Accumulation

phases.deload: Every 4 weeks an easier week, keeping 60 % of the volume.
phases.description: Volume comes down and intensity goes up, converting the accumulated capacity into usable power-endurance. Progress one lever at a time: less rest on bodyweight work or more load on barbell and kettlebell work — never both at once.
phases.intensity: Higher; one progression lever at a time
phases.name: Transmutation

phases.deload: Every 4 weeks an easier week, keeping 60 % of the volume.
phases.description: Low volume at peak intensity, so the qualities built in the previous blocks show up as performance. Recovery days stay in place; the mind is trained alongside the body.
phases.name: Realization

exercise.name: Wall Squat (Mobility Drill)
exercise.notes: Gym Jones warm-up staple used in virtually every strength and circuit session. Stand with toes touching a wall, feet wide. Drop into a squat with knees tracking toes; contact the wall with knees to enforce vertical shin position and upright torso. Hands brace against wall as needed. Builds ankle mobility, hip flexor opening, and thoracic extension. Not a strength exercise — a diagnostic and mobility drill. 2–3 sets of 5 before any lower body session.

exercises.notes: Wall squat mobility drill. 3×5 before any lower body session.

exercise.name: Air Squat
exercise.notes: CrossFit fundamental movement. Rippetoe squatting standards apply: below parallel, neutral spine, heels flat. Gym Jones warm-up protocol: 2×5 wall squats then 2×10 air squats before loading. Chelsea benchmark: 15 squats per minute EMOM 30 min.

exercises.notes: Unilateral squat strength. Single-leg squat (box) 5×5 each side. Progress by lowering box height toward pistol range. If box pistols are mastered, advance to weighted step-up.

exercise.name: Kettlebell Step-Up (Single-Arm)
exercise.notes: Single-arm kettlebell step-up. Hold one KB at the chest (rack) or goblet position. Drive through the heel of the lead foot; no assistance from the trailing leg. 5×2 each side at a heavy bell. KB step-up approximates the Gym Jones loaded step-up protocol when a barbell is unavailable. Box height governs difficulty — a higher box increases unilateral demand.

exercise.name: Plank Hold (FLR — Front Leaning Rest)
exercise.notes: Gym Jones programs 300-second accumulated FLR (Front Leaning Rest) as a core and shoulder endurance component. Maintain neutral spine; do not allow hip sag. Progress toward 5 continuous minutes before loading.
